ui.about.byMachine: Meet the machines and their facts
ui.about.byMachineNote: Open a machine to read every fact we used and the NASA page it came from.
ui.about.what: The Abandoned Explorers is an interactive 3D journey by Team Zorvex for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Kandy, Sri Lanka). Children play the true missions of machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, and learn the science each one made possible.
ui.about.sourcesNote: Every line a machine speaks rests on one of these facts, each checked against the linked source.
ui.about.aiNote: We used an AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) to help write code and draft text. People on the team checked every fact against the linked sources. The voices are AI-generated with the open Kokoro text-to-speech model (run on our own computer). There are no AI-generated images or models. The full log is in docs/AI_USAGE.md in our repository.
ui.about.disclaimer: NASA does not endorse this project. NASA imagery and data are used under NASA's media guidelines and credited to their sources.

parts.viking-lander.cameras.name: Cameras
parts.viking-lander.cameras.job: Two cameras turned in a full circle, scanning one thin line at a time.
parts.viking-lander.cameras.science: The first photos ever taken on the surface of Mars.
parts.viking-lander.arm.name: Sampler arm
parts.viking-lander.arm.job: Scooped up Martian soil, with a temperature sensor and a magnet.
parts.viking-lander.arm.science: On 28 July 1976 it fed the first soil into the laboratory.
parts.viking-lander.biology.name: Biology laboratory
parts.viking-lander.biology.job: Three tests looked for signs of life in the soil.
parts.viking-lander.biology.science: Strange chemistry, but no clear evidence of life.
parts.viking-lander.gcms.name: Chemistry laboratory
parts.viking-lander.gcms.job: Measured what the soil is made of.
parts.viking-lander.gcms.science: Iron-rich clay that gives off oxygen when wet. No organic molecules found.
parts.viking-lander.weather.name: Weather boom
parts.viking-lander.weather.job: Measured temperature, wind direction and wind speed.
parts.viking-lander.weather.science: Weather reports from the surface of another planet.
parts.viking-lander.rtg.name: Nuclear power (RTGs)
parts.viking-lander.rtg.science: Power that never needed the Sun, so it could work for years.
parts.viking-lander.legs.name: Legs and landing engines
parts.viking-lander.legs.job: Three legs and three engines set it down gently.
parts.viking-lander.legs.science: Parachute, then engines: the first truly successful landing on Mars.
parts.mer-opportunity.pancam.name: Pancam
parts.mer-opportunity.pancam.job: Two cameras on a mast, at a human geologist's eye height.
parts.mer-opportunity.pancam.science: Colour 3-D panoramas of Mars, picture by picture.
parts.mer-opportunity.rat.name: Rock Abrasion Tool
parts.mer-opportunity.rat.job: Grinding teeth brushed off dust and old rock.
parts.mer-opportunity.rat.science: Fresh rock underneath for the other tools to study.
parts.mer-opportunity.apxs.name: APXS
parts.mer-opportunity.apxs.job: Found which elements make up a rock.
parts.mer-opportunity.apxs.science: Clues about weathering and water on ancient Mars.
parts.mer-opportunity.mossbauer.name: Mössbauer spectrometer
parts.mer-opportunity.mossbauer.job: Found minerals that contain iron. One reading took about 12 hours.
parts.mer-opportunity.mossbauer.science: What the Martian environment was like long ago.
parts.mer-opportunity.microscope.name: Microscopic Imager
parts.mer-opportunity.microscope.job: Took extreme close-up pictures of rocks and soil.
parts.mer-opportunity.microscope.science: Tiny grains and textures, seen as if with a magnifying glass.
parts.mer-opportunity.solar.name: Solar panels
parts.mer-opportunity.solar.job: Sunlight gave the rover its power.
parts.mer-opportunity.solar.science: A dust storm covering all of Mars ended Opportunity's mission in 2018.
parts.insight-lander.seis.name: SEIS seismometer
parts.insight-lander.seis.job: Felt the ground shake, under a dome against wind and cold.
parts.insight-lander.seis.science: The pulse of Mars: marsquakes and meteorite thumps.
parts.insight-lander.hp3.name: HP3 heat probe (the mole)
parts.insight-lander.hp3.job: Meant to hammer almost 5 m down to measure heat from inside.
parts.insight-lander.hp3.science: The soil was different than expected, a lesson for future missions.
parts.insight-lander.rise.name: RISE radio
parts.insight-lander.rise.job: Radio tracking showed exactly where the lander was.
parts.insight-lander.rise.science: How Mars wobbles, and what its iron-rich core is like.
parts.insight-lander.arm.name: Robotic arm
parts.insight-lander.arm.job: Picked up the instruments and set them on the ground.
parts.insight-lander.arm.science: SEIS sat right on the ground, away from the lander.
parts.ingenuity.rotors.name: Rotors
parts.ingenuity.rotors.job: Blades about 1.2 m from tip to tip, spinning in very thin air.
parts.ingenuity.rotors.science: Up to 5 m high and 300 m far: flight on another planet.
parts.ingenuity.solar.name: Solar panel
parts.ingenuity.solar.job: Charged the batteries for one 90-second flight a day.
parts.ingenuity.body.name: Body and batteries
parts.ingenuity.body.science: Planned for five flights, it flew 72 times.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.engine.name: Descent engine
parts.apollo-lunar-module.engine.job: A rocket that could throttle down for a soft landing.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.engine.science: It landed the first people on the Moon.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.legs.name: Legs and footpads
parts.apollo-lunar-module.legs.job: Four legs held it 1.5 m above the dust.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.legs.science: Opposite footpads were 9.4 m apart for a steady stand.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.ladder.name: Ladder and porch
parts.apollo-lunar-module.ladder.job: The astronauts climbed down to the surface here.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.ladder.science: The first human footsteps on another world began on this ladder.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.cabin.name: Crew cabin
parts.apollo-lunar-module.cabin.job: Two astronauts, two triangular windows, and no seats.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.cabin.science: The top half flew them back up to orbit.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.sband.name: S-band antenna
parts.apollo-lunar-module.sband.job: Carried voice, TV and data to Earth.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.sband.science: How the world saw and heard the Moon landing.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.radar.name: Rendezvous radar
parts.apollo-lunar-module.radar.job: Helped the cabin find the Command Module in orbit.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.radar.science: Meeting another spacecraft around the Moon.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.rcs.name: Steering thrusters
parts.apollo-lunar-module.rcs.job: Sixteen small thrusters pointed it in any direction.
parts.apollo-lunar-module.rcs.science: Steering for flying and docking in space.
parts.pioneer-10.dish.name: Radio dish
parts.pioneer-10.dish.science: At Jupiter a command and its reply took up to 92 minutes.
parts.pioneer-10.rtg.name: Nuclear generators (RTGs)
parts.pioneer-10.rtg.job: Made electricity far from the Sun.
parts.pioneer-10.rtg.science: The first spacecraft powered only by nuclear energy.
parts.pioneer-10.magnetometer.name: Magnetometer
parts.pioneer-10.magnetometer.science: Jupiter's magnetic tail stretches all the way to Saturn's orbit.
parts.pioneer-10.camera.name: Imaging photopolarimeter
parts.pioneer-10.camera.job: Took pictures of Jupiter and its moons.
parts.pioneer-10.camera.science: About 500 pictures of Jupiter and its Great Red Spot.
parts.pioneer-10.plaque.name: The plaque
parts.pioneer-10.plaque.job: A message from Earth, engraved in metal.
parts.pioneer-10.plaque.science: It shows who made the spacecraft and where we live.
